A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same I-PERI research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 6 report original synthetic-data experiments comparing I-PERI's estimated CPDAG and Φ-CPDAG using SHD and F1.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original linear and nonlinear synthetic-data experiments, baseline comparisons, local-discovery-method comparisons, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The two-phase minimax-regret framework remains, but Equation (4) changes from intersecting the server graph with the client skeleton to undirected-consensus masking. Under the new rule, a server-directed edge becomes undirected in the mask when the client edge is undirected. This changes orientation-stage scoring beyond merely renaming the operator.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates linear Gaussian structural models only. V2 retains this coverage and adds nonlinear causal-discovery scenarios using randomly selected tanh, sine, and quadratic mechanisms in Appendix B, substantially extending the tested functional regimes.

E2.justification: V1's empirical comparison is between I-PERI's own CPDAG and Φ-CPDAG outputs. V2 adds evaluated comparisons against PERI, NOTEARS-ADMM, FedDAG, and FedCDH in Table 1 and the linear-data figures. These methods were not evaluated as baselines in v1.

E3.justification: The reported experimental grids change: Figure 6's client counts move from 3, 5, 10, 20 to 2, 4, 8, 10, and heterogeneous sample sizes change from 1000/2000/5000 to 500/1000/2000. Variable-count experiments extend to 20 variables. New nonlinear experiments introduce five-bin discretization and PC with a chi-squared independence test; SHD and F1 remain the evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The comparison between initial CPDAG recovery and orientation refinement is retained. V2 adds a targeted sensitivity analysis of the client discovery algorithm: Figure 8b directly compares PC and GES, alongside GES-based baseline experiments in Figure 8a.

E5.justification: V1 shows shaded bands without specifying their meaning or the run count. V2 reports averages over 10 seeds, means with standard deviations in Tables 1–2, and confidence intervals in figure captions. It also discloses selecting seeds to obtain client CPDAG F1 above 0.85. This substantially expands statistical reporting, although interval construction remains unspecified and an increase in runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: V2 replaces and expands the original phase-comparison curves with baseline, runtime, PC/GES, and nonlinear results. For example, linear Table 1 reports SHD 4.44 for I-PERI versus 8.40 for PERI at eight variables, whereas nonlinear Table 2 reports 9.33 versus 9.10. These are newly reported results under revised or added conditions, rather than established performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: The Φ-CPDAG definition expands from orienting intervened-graph v-structures to incorporating every oriented edge in client CPDAGs. Appendix A substantially revises the convergence arguments and replaces v1's citation-only sensitivity proof with an explicit derivation presented as correcting prior work. The displayed sensitivity bound itself is unchanged between versions.

C1.justification: The central contributions—unknown-intervention discovery, Φ-MEC identification, convergence, and privacy guarantees—remain. V2's introduction additionally calls Φ-MEC the best recoverable class under private, regret-only information exchange, strengthening v1's claim that it is a tighter equivalence class.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explicit limitation that inaccurate client CPDAGs, especially erroneous orientations, propagate into the server's Φ-CPDAG. It also explains that nonlinear applicability depends on the client discovery method. The existing causal-assumption limitations and interpretation of parametric interventions remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents PC and BIC use in the main experiments, the client intervention arrangement, nonlinear generation and preprocessing, and the chi-squared test. It also supplies a reproducibility-code link. These substantially extend v1's implementation information; the PDFs do not establish that newly disclosed choices were absent from the earlier implementation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its treatment of federated causal discovery into constraint-based, score-based, and optimization-based approaches, with numerous additional citations. It explicitly distinguishes its setting from Abyaneh et al.'s known-intervention federated work. The existing comparison with centralized unknown-intervention research is largely retained and moved into the introduction.

P1.justification: Existing introductory, methodological, and privacy passages are extensively rewritten. Related-work discussion moves from the discussion section to the introduction, masking and inclusion definitions move into Section 3, and the appendices receive explicit Proofs and Experimental Results sections. Terminology and explanations are revised throughout.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 are redrawn with separate client-graph and masking panels, and Figure 4 is rearranged. V1's Figure 5 and illustrative regret table are replaced by a different equivalence-class comparison and empirical tables. The experimental displays are substantially redesigned and expanded with runtime and appendix plots.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's lack of external empirical comparisons by adding four baselines, runtime measurements, nonlinear evaluation, and a client-method sensitivity check. Statistical reporting, implementation details, and the explicit local-accuracy limitation make the evidence easier to assess and reproduce. Seed selection for high local accuracy limits generalization, and broad dominance claims overstate Tables 1–2, including I-PERI's lower F1 than PERI at 20 variables in Table 1. Despite these weaknesses, the comparative validation and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.
